Karpeles Lab CEO Mark Karpelès on why criminals shifted to attacking hardware wallets, and why Ledger was likely hit first

"Self custody is here for a big reason. Computers get viruses and get hacked. One term we use a lot in IT security is attack surface. Which is basically what entry points there are into an IT system that allow someone to get inside."

"For a computer, you are connected to the Internet. You open a number of websites all day. Typically, you will be plugging devices, USB keys, inside your computer. So all of these things are risk factors."

"By having your private key and performing the signature on a separate device, which has a limited connectivity option, which basically limits the attack surface, you protect your cryptocurrencies from all those viruses or things that can infect your computer."

"I believe that self custody on cold wallets or hardware wallets has been successful and has reduced the crypto theft from virus enough for those criminal groups to move to find ways to attack those devices."

"Ledger having, the largest market share was probably the first target basically, where there was the most to gain. And that would make sense that Ledger was the first being attacked here."

AI agents can now book the hotel and order the cleats, as long as they're allowed to pay.

That's set off the "wallet wars," with major players racing to connect to agents:

- Stripe's Link: 300M users
- Shopify's Shop Pay: 250M users
- PayPal: 400M+ users

How your agent pays matters. If a wallet pays the store with its own stand-in card, the purchase goes through, but your card rewards, purchase protections, and relationship with the store can get lost along the way.

Say your agent books a United flight on your airline credit card. If the wallet pays United with its own virtual card, the money moves, and your miles may never show up.

Agents also have to pick the right card for each purchase, and when one books the wrong hotel dates, someone has to make it right.

Where it's all headed: new open standards from Visa, Mastercard, and Amex.

"The best of all worlds is a future where my agent can use my credit card, without having my credit card."

SG Summary:

Update: 10/12: Vol into CPI on Wednesday 10/14 is very low, and so we want to avoid being short of options into the print as well as OPEX. After Monday, an SPX move >7,825 has the potential to move up quickly due to negative gamma. Support is solid down in to 7,700. <7,700 we shift to a risk-off stance.

10/6: Despite higher yields, stocks are sliding higher. If those yields come down, then we may see strong moves higher in stocks. Given this, we think its critical to maintain upside exposure, and for that we prefer NVDA Nov of Dec calls as the IV rank for NVDA is <5.

Key SG levels for the SPX are:

Resistance: 7,830, 7,850, 7,900
Pivot: 7,690 (bearish <, bullish >) updated 9/22/26
Support: 7,800, 7,750, 7,700

Founder's Note:

Futures are flat ahead of bank earnings and home sales data at 10 AM EST. US10Y 5.19% from +5.3% last week.

The key positive gamma range noted the last several days remains in tact: 7,700 - 7,800. We do not think the market is poised to move much today, with CPI on deck tomorrow. 

That being said, the market does have a problem: a complete lack of volatility being priced in.  We want to be long of Nov options here as we think realized vol is poised to once again wake up - just as it did out of Sep OPEX. 

Starting with an indexified measure of vol, VIX1D, you can see it is at a lower bound of ~7. A backtest on this shows that forward SPY returns are essentially flat. It is not a signal of an explosive pending move. With CPI and earnings afoot, we think "this time may be different".

Stepping out farther in tenor, we see that SPX 3 month IV is also at nearly 2-year lows - this despite all of the things going on (wars, rates, elections).  And while you may not agree with wanting to be long of options here, we are hard pressed to find a reason why shorting them is worth the risk-reward.

About a month ago ago, out of Sep OPEX, we had remarked that volatility was poised to break out. That seemed to come to fruition as the Nasdaq broke 6% higher into October. Then, as rates ripped higher the equity market did something odd: it stalled (recall all those MOVE vs VIX conversations). Over that same time frame, traders seem to have also shifted from a META-driven AI hope, to tech-malaise. You can see that "wedge breakout" in realized vol from the SMH chart below - and you can also see the big fade. In fact this morning SMH is down another ~1.5% as Chinese memory/chip makers are allegedly increasing production. 

If the equity space loses a tech bid, some other sector clearly has to carry the bullish baton.  It's possible lower rates via a cool CPI could drive the lagging non-tech sector.  TSM earnings on 10/15 is the first major tech co to report, and on that point you can see that single stocks generally carry a rich IV (left), but the call skew has faded (right) as traders sour on tech. 

On the idea of shifting to other bullish vectors, you can see the put/call ratios for tech are indeed off highs (shades of red) while other, more beaten up sectors, are finding some higher relative call volumes. We're not sure if this is simply some bottom fishing or something more substantial, but its looks like a potential transition is underway. Consider XLF - its down 10% from its Aug 1 highs while seeing call-heavy volumes - particularly as rates come off (and major earnings this AM).

The wallet wars are here.

Very Good Security chief strategy officer Terry Angelos joins a16z's Alex Rampell, his TrialPay co-founder from back in 2006 (TrialPay was later acquired by Visa), to discuss how agents are learning to spend money.

"Agents have all of a sudden become significantly more helpful and useful because they effectively have arms and legs, which are payment credentials."

VGS holds the payment credentials behind about 1/3 of all e-commerce, and now it's helping AI agents pay merchants. If you've bought anything online, there's a good chance VGS has already helped keep your card safe.

In the last three months, Terry says agents went from "spectators to actors." Once an agent has your payment credentials, it can book the piano teacher it previously could only find and recommend.

Now Stripe's Link, Shopify's Shop Pay, and PayPal are racing to connect to agents. It's all headed toward open standards from the card networks: agentic tokens that let an agent pay with your actual card.

VGS went from zero agentic tokens to a few million a week in three months.

Mortgage lenders will lose far more during the developing mortgage crisis than they did during all of the GFC. From 2007–2010, realized losses on defaulted mortgages totaled about $450 billion.

There is currently about $8.3 trillion in outstanding fixed-rate mortgages with an average rate of 4.6% and 25 years left to maturity. Given that current rates are 7.5%, the mark-to-market losses on those mortgages are already about $2 trillion. When rates rise to 8.5%, the loss will rise to $3 trillion!

That means even without a single default, on paper mortgage lenders have already lost over four times more than they lost during the GFC. That loss will grow to nearly seven times as much when mortgage rates hit 8.5%.

Worse, during the GFC, since mortgage rates plunged, lenders had mark-to-market gains on all the outstanding mortgages that did not default. Since only 10% of the mortgages defaulted, those unrealized gains totaled about $1.75 trillion. That provided a huge cushion that today's mortgage lenders no longer have. In fact, when mark-to-market gains were taken into account, mortgage lenders actually made $1.3 trillion during the GFC.

The current situation is therefore orders of magnitude worse. The impending disaster was created by the Federal Reserve holding interest rates so low for so long, and the FHA and GSEs guaranteeing 30-year fixed-rate mortgages, which allowed borrowers to lock in such low rates for such long durations. That sowed the seeds for the perfect storm of financial destruction that is about to hit.

I’m not going to reveal whose track record is attached, but it’s funny how every market cycle produces the same characters, just with different names.

They’re usually charismatic, have hundreds of thousands of followers, a podcast or paid subscription service, and a few TV appearances, which somehow serve as proof of credibility for many of the less sophisticated people on X.

Here’s how it usually works. They catch a major trend early, make 200–300% on their own relatively small portfolio, sometimes worth just $100K, and become famous on X.

Their track record rarely goes back more than four years because it usually starts with the cycle itself.

By the time their followers arrive, the trend is already in full motion, often approaching its final stage. The followers pay for subscriptions, sometimes generating over $1M annually for the promoter, while taking most of the downside when the cycle turns.

Look at the attached track record. This stock market commentator, with only four years of history, has already gone from +30% YTD to −6%. That’s a 36-percentage-point reversal.

These are often not experienced investors. They’re promoters who happened to catch one trend and built an audience around it.

They sell dreams about the future, ignore valuations, and convince people that every fashionable company is the next big thing.

If you’re following someone with only a four-year track record and treating them like a market genius, you’re taking an enormous risk with your money.

Every cycle creates new geniuses. Very few survive the next one.

Yes, AI is rapidly advancing mathematics (and theoretical physics problems that are essentially mathematical). Like Ramanujan’s notebooks, human mathematicians will spend months (years?) poring over the stream of papers that AI effortlessly generates, hoping to verify and understand them, probably until math itself (via Lean) becomes a branch of computer science like almost everything else.

However, after math and physics, there is still a next scientific frontier: chemistry, and especially biology and medicine.

I mean, it was already the frontier, but it’s the next one too. AI can crush deterministic math problems on the computer, but biomedicine is a highly empirical, noisy, multivariate, and yet often predictable domain.

Thus, AI radically increases our ambitions in biomedicine. All the omics data, all the messy literature, it can all be synthesized and analyzed in a flash. This is what the labs mean when they talk about curing all diseases. The tooling is available to take cracks at biomedical problems previously thought impossible.

Midjourney is doing this, Chan Zuckerberg is doing this, Anthropic is doing this, but there will be so much more.

@Immusoft just presented clinical data at ASGCT on ISP-001 (the world's first engineered B cell therapy ever tested in a human being).

They take a patient's own B cells, reprogram them, and put them back in the body.

Those cells become miniature factories that continuously produce the enzyme MPS I patients are missing.

This means that there’s no more need for twice-weekly infusions and no more spike-and-crash enzyme levels. Your own cells are doing the work indefinitely.

The disease they're targeting, Hurler Syndrome, kills most patients within 10 years of diagnosis.

There is no cure and the current standard of care is either frequent infusions (forever) or a stem cell transplant that carries its own mortality risk.

The clinical data showed:
→ Favorable safety and tolerability
→ Measurable biochemical activity
→ Patients were safely re-dosed

They're now planning to expand into pediatric populations with CIRM backing the trial with up to $23M. The FDA has granted Orphan Drug, Rare Pediatric Disease, and Fast Track designations.

The implications go way beyond MPS I with every disease that needs sustained protein delivery suddenly having a new option on the table.

Exciting times in bio.
